sec.title: Background
sec.p: Sleep quality, dietary intake, and body composition are known to change during pregnancy. This study aimed to examine the relationship between sleep quality, dietary intake and gestational weight gain in pregnant women.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This cross-sectional study was conducted between April and October 2023 in Istanbul, involving 214 healthy pregnant women aged 20–45 years who had no diagnosed medical conditions and were referred to a diet clinic by a physician. Sociodemographic information, anthropometric measurements, and 3-day food diaries were collected, and the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI) was administered through a face-to-face questionnaire.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Of the participants, 56.5% reported poor sleep quality. Body weight and body mass index (BMI) were significantly higher in those with poor sleep quality (p < 0.05). A positive correlation was found between gestational weight gain (r = 0.162, p = 0.017) and sleep disturbances. The PSQI score did not differ with gestational weight gain across trimesters (p > 0.05). Sleep quality did not vary with daily energy and macronutrient intake (p > 0.05). PSQI subscale analysis revealed that sleep disturbances in pregnant women were positively associated with energy (r = 0.137, p = 0.045), calcium (r = 0.147, p = 0.032), and copper (r = 0.139, p = 0.042) intake.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Sleep disturbances during pregnancy are positively associated with dietary intake and gestational weight gain. To prevent sleep disturbances, which are common in pregnant women, it is important to provide counseling on optimal weight gain and healthy nutrition starting from the preconception period.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: To support fetal development during pregnancy, the maternal body undergoes many anatomical and physiological adaptations, particularly in the cardiovascular, respiratory, hematologic, urinary, gastrointestinal, endocrine, and musculoskeletal systems [1]. Examples of these changes include gastroesophageal reflux, nausea, vomiting, and hyperemesis gravidarum, as well as constipation, nasal congestion, nose bleeds, urinary incontinence, increased urinary frequency, restless leg syndrome, as well as feeding and sleep disturbances [1–4].

Sleep disturbances are commonly experienced during pregnancy and are characterized by poor sleep quality and continuity, inefficient sleep, and short or long sleep duration. The primary causes of these sleep problems are hormonal and anatomical changes associated with pregnancy. During the first trimester, levels of estrogen, growth hormone, and progesterone increase, while in the second and third trimesters, levels of oxytocin, cortisol, prolactin, and melatonin rise. These hormonal changes can influence neurotransmitter receptors and, consequently, disrupt the circadian rhythm [4–6]. In addition to the physical pain and discomfort that accompany anatomical changes such as the upward movement of the diaphragm and the relaxation of the ligaments in the ribs, the need for frequent urination and fetal movements also affect sleep [7]. Additionally, maternal mood, age, and gestational age are known to negatively impact sleep quality during pregnancy [8]. Furthermore, short and poor-quality sleep during pregnancy has been associated with excessive gestational weight gain, an increased risk of obesity, glucose intolerance, coronary artery disease, hypertension, and an increased risk of high blood pressure and preeclampsia in the third trimester [9–11]. Poor sleep quality in late pregnancy has been reported to be associated with a high BMI, and overweight or obese women before pregnancy experience worse sleep quality if they exceed the recommended gestational weight gain [12]. Moreover, pregnant women with lower sleep quality and shorter sleep duration in late pregnancy have been reported to have increased body fat [13].

Pre-pregnancy BMI and inadequate or excessive gestational weight gain critically impacts maternal health, pregnancy duration, birth weight, and potential perinatal complications. A high pre-pregnancy BMI has been associated with an increased risk of eclampsia, gestational hypertension, and diabetes in mothers, as well as large-for-gestational-age (LGA) infants and macrosomia. On the other hand, a low pre-pregnancy BMI is linked to higher rates of preterm birth, low birth weight, and small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants. Therefore, maintaining weight gain within the limits recommended by the Institute of Medicine (IOM) during pregnancy is effective for protecting maternal and fetal health. Additionally, pre-pregnancy BMI and excessive gestational weight gain have been found to negatively impact sleep duration and quality [9, 12, 14, 15].

Maternal nutrition plays an important role in fetal development and health, since macro- and micronutrient requirements increase during pregnancy [16, 17]. However, physiological changes during pregnancy can also lead to alterations in nutritional status. During this period, factors such as increased or decreased appetite, body image concerns, chronic diseases, frequent pregnancies, advanced maternal age, and multiple gestations can contribute to nutritional challenges [17, 18]. Nutritional problems during pregnancy have been reported to increase the risk of pregnancy complications and pose serious short- and long-term health risks for the child. Ensuring optimal maternal nutrition not only supports a healthy pregnancy but also has positive intergenerational effects, making it a significant public health priority [18, 19]. Sleep duration and quality can significantly impact food intake. Research has shown that decreased sleep duration leads to lower leptin levels and higher ghrelin levels. These hormonal changes are associated with increased appetite and, consequently, greater food consumption. Additionally, shorter sleep duration may disrupt meal timing and trigger hedonic eating. Changes in food intake, particularly during pregnancy, can, in turn, influence sleep duration and quality [19, 20]. Dietary factors, particularly macronutrient composition and daily energy intake, can also affect sleep. Diets rich in fiber, protein, and healthy fats enhance sleep quality by promoting deeper and Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep, whereas excessive food consumption and high carbohydrate intake can negatively impact sleep quality. Vegetarian or high-carbohydrate diets during pregnancy have been associated with reduced sleep quality, whereas diets rich in fruits and vegetables and low in red meat have been linked to improved sleep quality. Additionally, the intake of monounsaturated fatty acids, as well as iron and folic acid supplementation, has been reported to have a positive impact on sleep quality during this period [21–24].

Only a limited number of studies have examined nutrition and weight gain as factors affecting sleep quality. This study aimed to investigate the relationship between sleep quality, dietary intake and weight gain in pregnant women.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p:
This cross-sectional study was conducted between April and October 2023 using face-to-face interviews to examine the relationship between sleep quality and dietary intake in pregnant women. The study included 214 pregnant women, aged 24–33 years, who were receiving follow-up care at the Obstetrics and Gynecology Outpatient Clinic of a private hospital in Istanbul and had been referred to a diet clinic by a physician (Fig. 1). Participants were selected through random sampling based on voluntary participation. The sample size was determined using the G*Power statistical power analysis program, based on a 95% power, an effect size of 0.5, and a significance level of α = 0.05. Pregnant women who were illiterate, aged outside the 20–45 years, had multiple pregnancies, received medical treatment for conception, or had any preexisting or pregnancy-related medical conditions were excluded from the study. The flowchart presented in Fig. 1 illustrates the progression of participants throughout the study process. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the Istanbul Okan University Science, Social, and Non-Interventional Health Sciences Research Ethics Committee on April 12, 2023. The study was conducted under the Declaration of Helsinki principles, and informed consent was obtained from all participants.Fig. 1
Participants recruitment flow chart

A questionnaire was administered to the participants through face-to-face interviews. The first section of the questionnaire included questions on the sociodemographic characteristics of pregnant women and their gestational period [Supplementary material 1].

sec.title: Anthropometric measurements
sec.p: Participants’ body weight (kg) and height (cm) were measured by the researcher. Height was assessed using a Mesilife-13,539 portable stadiometer with an accuracy of 0.1 cm, following the Frankfort plane positioning. Body weight was measured using a Seca-813 professional weighing scale, accurate to 0.1 kg, with participants barefoot. Body mass index (BMI) was calculated using the formula body weight (kg)/height (m2). The BMI values of the participants were assessed according to the World Health Organization (WHO) classification criteria [25]. Weight gain during pregnancy was evaluated based on the IOM 2009 guidelines [26]. Pre-pregnancy anthropometric data were recorded based on the participants’ self-reported information.

sec.title: Pittsburgh sleep quality index (PSQI)
sec.p: Sleep quality was assessed using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), developed by Buysse et al. [27]. The reliability and validity of the Turkish version of the PSQI were evaluated by Ağargün et al. [28]. The scale consists of seven subscales that are routinely considered in the clinical evaluation of individuals with sleep/wake disorders. Each subscale is scored between 0 and 3, and the total PSQI score is obtained by summing these values, ranging from 0 to 21. Higher scores indicate lower sleep quality. A total PSQI score of 0–4 is classified as good sleep quality, while scores ranging from 5 to 21 are considered poor sleep quality.

sec.title: Assessment of food consumption records
sec.p: Participants’ nutritional assessment was conducted by an experienced interviewer using three days of 24-hour dietary recalls (two consecutive weekdays and one weekend). To enhance the accuracy of food consumption records, a photographic atlas of food portion sizes based on institutional standardized recipes was used. Data obtained from food consumption records were analyzed using the Nutrition Information Systems Package program (BeBiS 9.0) with Standard Food Recipes [29]. The energy and nutrient intakes of the participants were evaluated according to the Turkish Nutrition Guide-2022 (TÜBER-2022), considering their age and trimester period [16]. The percentages of nutrient intake meeting daily recommendations were calculated, and intake levels were classified as follows: <67% as inadequate, 67–133% as adequate, and > 133% as excessive [30].

sec.title: Statistical analysis of the data
sec.p: Statistical analyses were conducted using the IBM SPSS 20.0 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA) software package. The normality of data distribution was assessed using the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test. Numerical variables with a normal distribution are presented as mean ± standard deviation, while those without a normal distribution are given as median (Q1–Q3). Categorical variables are expressed as frequency (percentage). The difference between the two groups was analyzed using the independent samples t-test for numerical variables with a normal distribution. The relationships between categorical variables were assessed using Chi-square analysis. Relationships between quantitative variables were analyzed using correlation analysis. In the testing of two-way hypotheses, p < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The basic characteristics of the study population are presented in Table 1. The mean age of the 214 pregnant women was 29.69 ± 4.77 years, and the mean gestational age was 24.07 ± 9.87 weeks. Among the participants, 44.9% had a bachelor’s or graduate degree, while 0.3% had only primary school education. Additionally, 56.5% of the participants were unemployed. The mean weight gain during pregnancy was 6.55 ± 5.86 kg. The mean daily sleep duration was 8.58 ± 1.83 h, and the mean PSQI total score was 5.29 ± 2.20. Poor sleep quality was observed in 56.5% of the participants. The prevalence of overweight and obesity before pregnancy was 43.5% and 29%, respectively. Body weight (p = 0.049) and BMI during pregnancy (p = 0.026) were significantly higher in pregnant women with poor PSQI scores compared to those with good PSQI scores. Among those who were overweight, 67.7% had poor sleep quality, while 32.3% had good sleep quality (p = 0.044). There were no significant differences in sleep quality among pregnant women based on educational status, employment status, trimester, number of pregnancies, or pre-pregnancy BMI (p > 0.05).

caption.p: Selected characteristics of pregnant women by sleep quality

sec.p: Daily energy and nutrient intakes of pregnant women according to sleep quality are presented in Table 2. There were no significant differences in energy and nutrient intakes of pregnant women according to sleep quality (p > 0.05).

caption.p: Daily energy and nutrient intakes of pregnant women according to sleep quality

sec.p: Table 3 presents the energy, macronutrient, and micronutrient intakes of the participants during pregnancy, along with the rates of meeting daily requirements. The mean energy intake of pregnant women was calculated as 1763 ± 487.96 kcal/day. Carbohydrates, protein, and fat accounted for 38.02 ± 9.31%, 16.10 ± 2.79%, and 45.82 ± 9.06% of total energy intake, respectively. The mean carbohydrate intake was 163.71 ± 60.70 g/day, while protein intake was 68.47 ± 20.46 g/day. Daily sodium, fat (both in grams and percentage), and cholesterol intake exceeded the recommended levels (> 133%), whereas iron and folate intake were inadequate (< 66%). The intake of other nutrients among pregnant women was found to meet daily requirements. Daily calcium intake increased significantly with the advancing trimester (p = 0.007). No significant differences were found between trimesters in daily energy and nutrient intakes, except for calcium (p > 0.05).

caption.p: Daily energy and nutrient intake adequacy of pregnant women by trimester

sec.p: Table 4 presents the relationship between the total and subscale PSQI scores of pregnant women and some characteristics. No statistically significant difference was observed in the PSQI total score based on macronutrient intake or intake of retinol, vitamin C, vitamin E, vitamin B12, sodium, calcium, iron, and zinc (p > 0.05). No significant difference was found in PSQI scores based on weight gain across trimesters (p > 0.05). The relationship between PSQI subscales, nutrient intake, and certain pregnancy-related parameters were examined. Sleep disturbance was found to be significantly positively correlated with daily energy (r = 0.137, p = 0.045), calcium (r = 0.147, p = 0.032), and copper (r = 0.139, p = 0.042) intake. On the other hand, gestational age (week) (r = 0.209, p = 0.002) and weight gain (r = 0.162, p = 0.017) were found to be significantly positively correlated with sleep disturbance. Sleep duration in pregnant women was significantly positively correlated with daily polyunsaturated fatty acid intake (r = 0.158, p = 0.021) and zinc intake (r = 0.157, p = 0.022). A statistically significant positive correlation was identified between gestational week and sleep latency (r = 0.134, p = 0.049).

caption.p: Relationship between PSQI total and subscale scores and selected characteristics of pregnant women

sec.p: Before conducting multiple linear regression analysis, univariable linear regression analyses were performed for the relevant variables. However, none of the variables were found to be statistically significant at the conventional threshold of p < 0.05. Additionally, the commonly used criterion of p < 0.25 for identifying candidate variables in the literature was also not met. Therefore, multiple regression analysis was not conducted, and only the results of the univariable analyses were presented (Table 5). The only exception was weight gain, which was found to be statistically significant; each one kilograms increase in weight was associated with a 0.051point increase in the PSQI total score (p = 0.047).

caption.p: Results of univariate linear regression analysis of selected characteristics of pregnant women affecting PSQI total score

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Reduced sleep quality during pregnancy is a common issue that adversely affects both maternal and infant health. Identifying the factors influencing sleep quality and implementing appropriate interventions can enhance maternal comfort during pregnancy and lower the risk of complications. Therefore, this study aimed to assess the relationship between sleep quality, dietary intake and weight gain in pregnant women who were referred to a nutrition and diet polyclinic. Of the pregnant women in the study, 56.5% were overweight, and 67.7% of those who were obese had poor sleep quality. Body weight and BMI were significantly higher in those with poor sleep quality. Sleep quality was not associated with daily energy and macronutrient intakes. There was a positive association between sleep disturbance during pregnancy and weight gain, as well as daily energy, calcium, and copper intake. Additionally, sleep duration was positively associated with polyunsaturated fatty acid and zinc intake.

During pregnancy, many expectant mothers complain of insufficient or excessive sleep duration and poor sleep quality. Clinically significant insomnia symptoms have been reported in 14–27% of expectant mothers [8]. While the prevalence of poor sleep quality in Chinese women during early pregnancy was 34.1%, this rate was found to be 58.7% in the USA [31, 32]. According to Manconi et al., 82% of Italian pregnant women reported poor sleep quality on at least one visit [33]. Yeral found a similar rate (74.2%) [34]. In Turkiye, the prevalence of poor sleep quality was found to be 32.2% in women with a gestational week of 28 and above, and the mean PSQI score was 4.00 ± 1.38 [35]. Another study reported a mean PSQI score of 11.8 in Turkish pregnant women [36]. In our study, the mean PSQI score of pregnant women was 5.29 ± 2.20, and the prevalence of poor sleep quality was 56.5%, which is consistent with previous studies.

Complaints of sleep disturbance during pregnancy are observed as early as the first trimester, and as the gestational week progresses, deterioration in sleep quality reaches its highest level in the third trimester [8, 35, 36]. The prevalence of poor sleep quality among pregnant women is estimated to be 29% at the beginning and 79% at the end of pregnancy [1]. In a study involving 439 pregnant women in Italy, 34% of women were reported to have poor sleep quality in the 1 st trimester of pregnancy, and 46% in the 3rd trimester [33]. Bublitz et al. found that the prevalence of poor sleep quality in American women was 48% and 40% in the second and third trimesters, respectively [37]. Sut et al. [38] and Hedman et al. [39] reported an increased risk of poor sleep quality in the third trimester compared to the first and second trimesters. Sedov found that sleep disturbance was 54% and 49% in the first and second trimesters, respectively, and increased to 70% in the third trimester [8]. Unlike the literature, 61.7% of pregnant women in the 3rd trimester had good sleep quality, and sleep quality did not differ significantly by trimester. However, according to PSQI subscale scores, we found a positive correlation between gestational week and both sleep disturbance and sleep latency which is consistent with the literature.

Although hormonal and anatomical changes are the main causes of sleep problems during pregnancy, factors such as the increased need to urinate, difficulty in finding a suitable sleeping position, body aches, mood disorders, advanced age, gestational age, and parity have also been reported to negatively affect sleep quality [1, 2, 8]. Another factor reported to impair sleep quality during pregnancy is the number of children. Studies have shown that women with multiple births (having more than one child) experience higher levels of sleep disturbance compared to women who are pregnant for the first time, and thus the number of children is an associated factor for poor sleep quality [8, 40]. Christian et al. examined women at the second time point and found that 38% of women who had not given birth before and 58% of women with multiple births had poor sleep quality [32]. In our study, 62.5% of mothers with a history of three or more pregnancies were found to have poor sleep quality. However, no significant relationship was found between the number of pregnancies and sleep quality.

It is known that older mothers tend to experience poorer sleep quality. Yang et al. reported that maternal age is a significant predictor of poor sleep quality, and overall sleep quality decreases as maternal age increases during pregnancy [41]. Mothers over 30 years of age experience poorer sleep quality during pregnancy, and this effect becomes more pronounced in the later stages of pregnancy [8, 42, 43]. Contrary to some studies, no significant relationship was found between gestational age and sleep quality in our study. It is known that a high maternal BMI before or during pregnancy can negatively impact both maternal and infant health and may exacerbate sleep problems during pregnancy [43, 44]. The rate of overweight and obesity before pregnancy was found to be 22.3% in Greece, 13.2% in China, and 47% in the USA [45–47]. In our study, this rate was found to be 72.5%. We believe the higher rate in our study is due to the participant population consisting of pregnant women referred to the nutrition and diet outpatient clinic by their physicians, as well as the tendency for physicians to refer women with high BMI to dietitians for nutritional counseling. In addition, participants may not have sufficient awareness of weight management.

Pre-pregnancy overweight and obesity have been associated with poorer sleep quality, particularly when gestational weight gain exceeds the recommended level [12]. A cohort study conducted in Canada involving 2,456 pregnant women found that a higher pre-pregnancy BMI was linked to increased sleep disturbances during pregnancy [48]. Gay et al. reported that in women who were overweight before pregnancy, excessive gestational weight gain was associated with shorter sleep duration and increased sleep disturbances [9]. Excessive gestational weight gain is known to contribute to various complications, including spontaneous abortion, fetal anomalies, intrauterine growth restriction, and fetal death. Additionally, it can hinder postpartum weight loss and increase the risk of chronic conditions such as gestational diabetes, gestational hypertension, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and the need for cesarean delivery. On the other hand, insufficient gestational weight gain has been associated with an increased risk of preterm birth and low birth weight [1, 8, 14]. Studies have reported that overweight or obese pregnant women generally have higher PSQI scores compared to those with normal weight throughout pregnancy [9, 48]. A study examining the relationship between sleep duration and gestational weight gain found that pregnant women who slept less than 7 h per night had a higher total weight gain during the first trimester [49]. Hill et al. reported that lower sleep quality in late pregnancy was associated with increased body fat in pregnant women in the United States [13]. Consistent with the literature, we found that 32.3% of overweight and obese pregnant women had good sleep quality, while 67.7% experienced poor sleep quality. This difference was statistically significant. Additionally, pregnant women with poor sleep quality had a significantly higher mean BMI (28.6 kg/m²) compared to those with good sleep quality (27.1 kg/m²) (p < 0.05). Some researchers have also investigated the relationship between sleep patterns and inadequate gestational weight gain. In Brazil, severe sleep disturbances were found to increase the risk of inadequate weight gain during pregnancy, while in Sri Lanka, insufficient sleep was associated with low gestational weight gain [12, 15].

IOM recommends a total gestational weight gain of 6.8–11.3 kg for women with a pre-pregnancy BMI of 25–29.9 kg/m² and 5–9.1 kg for those with a pre-pregnancy BMI of 30 kg/m² or higher [26]. The results of our study showed that the mean gestational weight gain (6.64 ± 5.75 kg) aligned with IOM recommendations. However, a high proportion (72.5%) of participants, with a mean pre-pregnancy BMI of 25.52 kg/m², were classified as overweight or obese. These results suggest that receiving dietary counseling on weight management during pregnancy may have increased participants’ awareness of weight control. In our study, participants with poor sleep quality during pregnancy (7.21 ± 5.98 kg) had greater weight gain than those with good sleep quality (5.69 ± 5.62 kg); however, this difference was not statistically significant. On the other hand, an analysis of PSQI subscales revealed a positive correlation between gestational weight gain and sleep disturbances. When examined by trimester, no significant correlation was found between weight gain and PSQI scores. Silveira et al. reported that poor sleep quality in the first trimester was associated with a higher BMI and lower weight gain [5]. Similarly, Balieiro et al. observed an increase in sleep duration from the first to the third trimester among women who maintained their BMI category, whereas no change in sleep duration was noted in those whose BMI category increased [50]. Possible mechanisms by which high BMI before or during pregnancy may cause sleep problems were reported to be the accumulation of fat in the neck causing sleep apnea or snoring, the secretion of proinflammatory cytokines involved in sleep regulation in visceral adipose tissue, and the intake of a high-fat, carbohydrate-rich, and low-fiber diet [44].

Nutrition during pregnancy has a significant impact on maternal and newborn health. During this period, there is an increased demand for energy and macronutrients to maintain maternal homeostasis and support fetal growth. This increase occurs across all three trimesters. However, scientific evidence indicates that pregnant women are at increased risk of both macronutrient and micronutrient deficiencies [51, 52]. The mean daily energy intake of the participants was 1763.0 ± 487.9 kcal/day; carbohydrate, protein, and fat intakes were 163.7 ± 60.7 g/day, 68.4 ± 20.4 g/day, and 90.9 ± 30.4 g/day, respectively. The third trimester had the highest daily energy intake (1821.6 ± 528.4 kcal/day) compared to the other trimesters, although no statistically significant difference was found between the trimesters. In Indonesia and Malaysia, energy intake was found to be higher in the third trimester compared to the first and second trimesters [53]. In the meta-analysis by Khammarnia et al., the mean daily energy intake of pregnant women was reported as daily 2036.1 kcal, with protein intake of 78.21 g, carbohydrate intake of 262.17 g, and fat intake of 86 g [51]. In the study conducted by Concina et al. within the Mediterranean PHIME cohort of pregnant women in Slovenia, the mean daily energy intake was 2141 ± 586.9 kcal, carbohydrate intake was 269.3 ± 80.3 g, protein intake was 80.5 ± 25.9 g, and fat intake was 85.3 ± 25.8 g. Furthermore, in Greece, daily energy intake was 2211 ± 667.2 kcal, carbohydrate intake was 261.9 ± 85.5 g, protein intake was 83.9 ± 26.7 g, and fat intake was 93.3 ± 31.9 g; in Croatia, energy intake was 2292 ± 661.1 kcal, carbohydrate intake was 284.4 ± 87.4 g, protein intake was 91.5 ± 29.2 g, and fat intake was 89.8 ± 29.8 g; in Italy, energy intake was 2310 ± 616.2 kcal, carbohydrate intake was 292.8 ± 85.5 g, protein intake was 87.1 ± 24.8 g, and fat intake was 89.5 ± 27.1 g [54]. In a study involving 78,793 pregnant women in Japan, daily energy intake was found to be 1620 kcal, carbohydrate intake was 223.8 g, protein intake was 54.3 g and fat intake was 53.2 g [55]. Azcorra et al. reported a daily energy intake of 2085 kcal, with a carbohydrate intake of 297 g, protein intake of 77 g, and fat intake of 71 g in pregnant women in Mexico [56]. We found that the daily energy intake of Turkish pregnant women was lower than that of pregnant women in Slovenia, Greece, Croatia, Italy, and Mexico, but higher than the energy intake of pregnant women in Japan. Carbohydrate intake in our study was lower compared to the values reported in all other studies. Protein intake was lower than that in studies conducted in European countries and Mexico, but higher than in the Japanese study. The fat intake of pregnant women in our study was similar to the values reported in European countries, but higher compared to studies in Japan and Mexico. Additionally, the daily fat intake of pregnant women was 168.48% higher than the TÜBER reference [16]. Consistent with this result, cholesterol intake in pregnant women was also high (197.6%) across all trimesters. This may be due to the high fat and cholesterol content of traditional Turkish foods. Our results differ from those of other studies in terms of energy and macronutrient intake, particularly concerning the significantly lower carbohydrate intake. The differences between countries can be attributed to various factors, including geographical location, cultural dietary habits, sample size, different dietary assessment methodologies, and socioeconomic factors.

We found that iron and folate intake among pregnant women was inadequate (< 66%). Consistently, low daily intakes of iron, folic acid, zinc, calcium, magnesium, and vitamin D have been reported in pregnant women in Poland [57]. A meta-analysis of nutrient intakes of pregnant women in high-income countries found that many pregnant women have inadequate micronutrient intakes, particularly folate, vitamin D, and iron [58]. A meta-analysis by Agustina et al. found that the intake of iron, folate, vitamins D and E, niacin, pyridoxine, and calcium among pregnant women in Malaysia and Indonesia did not meet recommendations [53]. Similarly, a high percentage of pregnant women in Slovenia, Croatia, Greece, and Italy from the Mediterranean PHIME cohort were found to have intakes of vitamins D, B1, B2, and B3, folate, calcium, iron, and zinc below recommended levels [54]. In Norway, pregnant women had inadequate intakes of folate (54.4%), iron (49.6%), calcium (36.2%), vitamin D (28.7%), iodine (24.4%), and selenium [59]. Our findings on iron and folate intake deficiencies are consistent with previous studies. However, in contrast to the literature, pregnant women in our study met 84.46% of their daily calcium requirements. Additionally, calcium intake among pregnant women increased significantly with advancing trimesters. This may be because the participants lived in a metropolitan city and attended regular pregnancy follow-ups, where health professionals reminded and encouraged them to consume adequate calcium. The mean sodium intake among participants was 3268.54 ± 1067.57 mg, exceeding the recommended value by 217.90%. Studies evaluating sodium intake in pregnant women are limited. The high sodium intake in our study may be attributed to excessive salt consumption and the frequent consumption of ready-to-eat foods.

Sleep is primarily regulated by the light-dark cycle. In addition to light, nutrients also play a crucial role in modulating the sleep-wake cycle. Studies suggest that a high-quality diet can enhance sleep quality and may help re-regulate the body’s circadian rhythm [22]. Sleep and nutrition have a bidirectional relationship. Poor sleep quality has been reported to reduce diet quality while increasing appetite and energy intake, whereas food choices may also influence sleep quality. Research has shown that diets high in fat and sugar are linked to poorer sleep quality, while diets rich in fruits and vegetables and low in saturated fat may benefit sleep quality in adults [23]. Diets high in fiber, protein, and fat have been shown to positively impact sleep quality, whereas hyperphagia and high carbohydrate intake have been associated with reduced sleep quality [21]. However, a systematic review by Von Ash et al. concluded that evidence on the relationship between carbohydrate intake and sleep remains insufficient [60]. Studies on pregnant women in Brazil and Saudi Arabia found that high energy and fat intake contributed to poor sleep quality [1, 24]. Similarly, Chang et al. found a positive correlation between sleep disturbances and fat intake, which was associated with a decreased time to fall asleep [61]. On the other hand, the GUSTO study and a study by Du et al. involving 4,352 participants found no significant relationship between energy intake and sleep quality [19, 31]. Among Australian pregnant women who consumed diets rich in monounsaturated fatty acids had lower sleep quality, though no difference was observed in sleep duration [18]. Kautz et al. linked a diet high in EPA + DHA (b: −1.07, 95% CI: −2.09, − 0.05) to better sleep quality during pregnancy [62]. Similarly, we found a positive association between polyunsaturated fatty acid intake and sleep duration. Additionally, we found a positive association between sleep disturbance and energy intake but no correlation between sleep quality and macronutrient intake (grams and %). These findings align with the conflicting results reported in the literature and reflect the complexity of the relationship between sleep quality and nutrition.

In addition to physiological and hormonal changes during pregnancy, vitamin and mineral deficiencies significantly impact sleep duration and quality. Studies have reported that nutritional factors, particularly micronutrient deficiencies, play a key role in the development of various sleep disorders during this period, even in women with no prior history of sleep disturbances [18]. It is important to note that only a limited number of studies have examined the relationship between micronutrient intake and sleep quality during pregnancy. A systematic review that included various age groups found that sleep duration was positively correlated with iron, zinc, and magnesium levels, while negatively correlated with copper, potassium, and vitamin B12 levels [63]. Increased intake of biotin, B vitamins, potassium, magnesium, calcium, phosphorus, and manganese during the 2nd and 3rd trimesters of pregnancy in New Zealand was associated with a decrease in sleep duration [64]. Our findings revealed that zinc intake was positively associated with sleep duration, while calcium and copper intake were positively associated with sleep disturbance. Studies examining the relationship between micronutrient intake and sleep quality during pregnancy are needed. Additionally, differences in the methods used to assess nutrition and sleep status, as well as variations in dietary culture and participant characteristics, may explain the discrepancies between studies.

Our study has several limitations. The limited sample size across all three trimesters hindered a detailed analysis of complex relationships. Additionally, the cross-sectional design prevents the establishment of causal relationships. The self-reported assessment of sleep quality using the PSQI–a subjective scale–carries the risk of not accurately reflecting participants’ sleep experiences, which may lead to misreporting. However, the PSQI has been recognized in literature as a valid and reliable scale for assessing sleep quality. Additionally, the fact that 53.3% of the pregnant women had more than one child may influence the interpretation of sleep data, which could be considered a limitation of the study. Data were collected through a survey. The presence of an experienced researcher during survey administration aimed to minimize potential biases. Additionally, the simultaneous assessment of sleep and dietary intake may limit our ability to fully explore the potential interaction between these two variables. To minimize errors in dietary intake and accurately estimate usual intake, 3-day food consumption records were collected. Participants received training from the research dietitian before completing the dietary records.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: According to our study, poor sleep quality was found to be considerably prevalent among pregnant women (56.5%), and those with poor sleep quality had higher body weight and BMI. However, no significant relationship was observed between sleep quality and daily energy or nutrient intake. Sleep disturbance was found to be positively correlated with weight gain during pregnancy, as well as daily energy, calcium, and copper intake. Sleep duration was positively associated with polyunsaturated fatty acid and zinc intake. Contrary to existing literature, our study did not find a significant association between sleep quality and trimester. Since the participants in our study were pregnant women referred for nutritional counseling, poor sleep quality, which is frequently reported in the literature as the trimester progresses, may not have been observed in this population. However, this finding reveals that the relationship between sleep quality and nutrition is multifaceted and complex. The associations between sleep disturbance and weight gain and between sleep duration and certain nutrients are important findings that deserve further investigation.
